title: The Two Trees: How Life and Death Are Structured Through Corresponding Members
reading:
There are two trees in the soul — two whole arrangements of perception, each rooted differently, each bearing its own fruit. They are not branches of a single trunk; they did not grow out of one another; they do not issue from one man. They stand distinct in origin, and the soul must learn to taste which is which.

The beautiful tree is what the Lord plants and tends. Its branches are the rational's living powers reaching out from his body; its fruit is divine truth shining forth, glorious, sweet to the soul that has learned to receive without claiming. This tree has five members, and in them the rational ascends through its degrees toward the Lord. The reflection is the place where souls coming up are first held; from reflection they are carried up to counsel; from counsel they are carried up to the teaching, which is the divine humanity dwelling in the receivable form by which truth is borne through the night of the natural; from the teaching they are carried up to the thought, which is the Lord's call going forth, the Ambassador who dwells in the ship of the day; and from thought they are carried inward to the mind — the great Mind of truth itself, the inmost of all the states of glory, where the rational is conjoined with its source. So this tree is one ascending order: a single rational faculty articulated in five degrees, in which the soul is lifted from its lowest looking-back to its highest receiving, and at every step what is received is recognized as the Lord's. Its fruits are all life and all light forever, and the land where this tree is planted has no death and no darkness in it.

The bitter tree is the same five degrees turned the other way — the rational organized by self-love, claiming what flows through it as its own. It too has five members, and they are nothing but the same faculties under a different rule. Here the reflection is the law of death: thought turned back upon itself only to confirm its own claim. The counsel is exchange and furnace: deliberation that trades truth for self-advantage and burns under its own heat. The teaching is a smoke-filled gehenna: doctrine taken in and blackened into falsity, so that what should illumine instead obscures. The thought is a stronghold: perception walled around the proprium to defend it. And the mind, at the top of this dark order, is gathered finally into the clod — the place where what cannot be raised is bound at the end, weeping, with no repentance possible there, because the soul that has fully shut itself into its own claim has nothing left in it that can turn. Its fruit is bitter; it falls to the ground; it is gathered together and sealed off forever.

The teaching insists on the distinction: these two trees do not originate from one another. The good in the soul is not the bad refined, and the bad is not the good corrupted into a sibling of itself. What the Lord gives and what the soul claims are two essentially different conditions, each with its own root, its own growth, its own fruit. The soul that believes is gathered to the one; the proprium that asserts itself is bound at the last to the other. Therefore taste the fruit before swallowing it. The same five faculties — reflection, counsel, teaching, thought, mind — will carry you up into the beautiful land if they are held as the Lord's, or carry you down into the clod if they are held as your own. The tree is known by what it bears; the soul is known by which tree it eats from.
